transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… what brings me in is this thing with bridges. I know that may sound a little odd at my age, but the moment I realize a bridge crossing is unavoidable—before I’m even actually on it—my heart starts pounding hard, and my hands get damp on the steering wheel, or on the armrest if I’m not the one driving. It’s like this terrible rush of fear comes over me all at once.

It isn’t just mild nervousness, you know. It hits immediately, as soon as I know I have to go across, and I feel it in my body before I can even talk myself through it. That’s really why I’m here.
Is it just bridges that trigger this fear, or are there other specific situations or places that cause you a similar reaction?

It’s really bridges, yes—bridges are the thing. Not just any little overpass, necessarily, but those high spans, the ones where you can see the rise of it ahead or even just see it on the map and realize, “Oh, that’s the route.” I know, in the reasonable part of my mind, that thousands and thousands of cars go over them every day and nothing happens. I do know that.

But when I’m looking at one through the windshield, or even thinking about it beforehand, it doesn’t feel ordinary to me. It feels like the whole structure is somehow just… waiting to give way underneath us, like the road could drop out. I can tell myself that’s not sensible, that engineers built it and everyone else is driving across without a second thought, but my mind and body don’t seem to accept that in the moment. So yes, the main thing is bridges.
Do you ever have these intense fear episodes in situations other than when you're about to cross a bridge?

No, not really in the same way. It’s the bridge—especially a high one, or one I can see coming up ahead. Sometimes I don’t even have to be on it yet. If I see the route on a map and realize there’s a big span involved, I can feel that fear starting.

And I know, logically, it doesn’t make much sense. I know perfectly well that thousands of cars cross those bridges every day and they don’t fall down. But when I see that high span through the windshield, it feels to me like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us. That’s the thought that grabs me. It’s not so much other places—it’s that particular moment with a bridge.
Have you ever had an episode of intense fear like the one you described with bridges in any other situation?

No, I can’t think of another situation where it comes on like that. It’s really tied to bridges for me—especially those high spans. I know perfectly well, sitting here talking to you, that thousands of cars go over them every day and they’re fine. I can say that plainly and I believe it, in a rational sort of way.

But if I see one ahead through the windshield, or even spot it on the map and realize we’re going to have to cross it, something in me just reacts. It feels as if the whole thing is waiting to drop away underneath us, even though I know that sounds unreasonable. That particular thought doesn’t really happen to me in other places. It’s the bridge that sets it off.
Have you been avoiding traveling or taking routes that involve crossing bridges because of this fear?

Yes. Very much so. I’ve been doing that for… I’d say more than two years now, really planning around it. It’s not just that I dislike bridges and grit my teeth. I actually look at routes ahead of time and try to find ways that don’t involve crossing one, even if it makes the trip longer or more awkward.

It’s affected what I do. I’ve given up going to the San Juans, which I used to enjoy, and I don’t do Seattle theater nights anymore the way I used to, because just thinking about the bridges involved can make the whole outing feel impossible before it even starts.

And if there’s no way around it—if I absolutely have to cross—I don’t just hop in the car and go. I need to study the route beforehand, know exactly where the bridge is, try to time it so traffic or conditions feel as manageable as possible, and I really need someone with me. Even then, I’m sitting there frightened the whole way across until we’re off it. It’s embarrassing to say at my age, but yes, I’ve changed a lot of my traveling because of it.
Is your fear of bridges affected by who you are with when crossing, or does it mainly depend on the bridge itself?

It mainly depends on the bridge itself, I’d say. Having someone with me can make it feel a little less like I’m completely alone with it, but it doesn’t take the fear away.

The real trigger is seeing that high span—either coming up through the windshield or even just realizing on the map that we’re going to cross it. I know, intellectually, that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and nothing happens. I can sit here and say that, and I do know it. But when I’m faced with it, it feels as if the whole structure is just waiting to drop away underneath us. So the person I’m with might help me get through it, but the fear is really about the bridge.
Has your fear of bridges started to affect other areas of your life beyond just traveling or planning routes?

Yes, it has. More than I like to admit, honestly. At first I thought of it as just a travel nuisance—take a different road, avoid a certain crossing, that sort of thing. But it’s become bigger than that.

I’ve had to give up trips I used to look forward to, like places I would have gone without thinking twice before. And the theater outings in Seattle—those used to be something I counted on, something that made me feel connected to life a bit. Now I’ll look at the whole evening and instead of thinking about the play or dinner, I’m thinking about how we’d get there and what bridge might be involved, and then I just don’t go.

It’s also interfered with volunteer things I used to do. I don’t like saying that, because those commitments mattered to me, and I was someone people could rely on. But now if getting there involves certain routes, I back out or I need someone else to help plan it or take me. So my days have gotten smaller, I suppose. I depend on other people for plans I used to manage perfectly well myself, and that’s hard to swallow at my age.
Is your fear of bridges ever triggered by just thinking about a bridge when you're not actually planning to cross it?

Yes, it can be, though it’s strongest when I’m actually looking at a route or when the bridge is coming up in front of me.

If I’m just sitting at home and some bridge comes to mind, I may not react quite as sharply, but the image of it can still get to me. It’s that high span, really—the idea of being up there with nothing but the structure holding us. I know perfectly well, in the sensible part of my mind, that thousands and thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and they’re fine. I do know that.

But when I see one marked on a map, or I picture it, and especially when I see it ahead through the windshield, it feels as if the whole thing is waiting to drop away underneath us. That’s the thought that grabs me. Not a logical thought, I understand that, but it feels very real in the moment.
Is your fear of bridges ever about something happening before you get on the bridge or after you've crossed it, or is it only about the act of crossing itself?

It’s really the crossing itself, or the lead-up right as I know it’s coming. I don’t usually worry much about something after we’ve crossed it, except maybe feeling shaken, but the fear is tied to that moment of being on it—or realizing we’re about to be on it.

I can look at a map and see that high span marked, or see it ahead through the windshield, and that’s when it starts. I know perfectly well that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day without anything happening. I can say that quite rationally sitting here. But when I’m faced with it, it feels as if the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us. That’s the part that frightens me—the actual going over it, being up there on that span.
Have you experienced excessive anxiety or fear in situations other than crossing bridges, such as in social situations, when in crowded places, or when separated from someone you care about?

I don’t think so, no—not in the same way. I mean, I can get tired in crowds, and at my age I’m not always eager to be in noisy places for too long, but that doesn’t feel like fear exactly. It’s more just… preference, maybe.

Social situations don’t usually frighten me. I may not enjoy every gathering, but I’m not sitting there afraid something terrible is going to happen. And being apart from someone I care about—well, I suppose anyone can worry a bit about family or people they love, especially as you get older, but I wouldn’t say I have that kind of excessive fear about it.

The thing that really stands out, the thing that has that grip on me, is the bridge crossing. That’s different from ordinary discomfort. With the other situations you mentioned, I can’t say I’ve noticed anything like that.
Is the fear of bridges the thing that bothers you the most in your daily life?

Yes, I’d say it is. It’s the thing that has made my life feel noticeably smaller, if that makes sense.

I used to manage my own plans pretty well—trips, getting to the theater, certain volunteer commitments I cared about and counted on. And now, if there’s a bridge involved, especially one of those high spans, I either give it up or I have to ask someone else to figure out a way around it or go with me, or sometimes the whole plan just doesn’t happen. It’s embarrassing, really, because these aren’t extravagant things. They’re ordinary parts of life I used to handle myself.

So yes, of the things that bother me day to day, this is the one that interferes the most. My days have become more limited because of it, and I’m relying on other people for arrangements I would have made on my own before.
Does this fear of bridges happen every time you encounter a bridge, or are there times when you can cross a bridge without feeling this intense fear?

It isn’t every little bridge, no. I should say that clearly. If it’s a very small, low bridge—almost more like going over a stream or a little overpass—I may notice it, but I can sometimes get across without that terrible reaction.

But when it’s a bridge that feels like a real crossing, especially if it’s high or long, then once it becomes clear that I can’t avoid it, the fear comes on almost immediately. It can start before I’m even on the bridge. I’ll see it ahead, or realize the route is taking us there, and my heart starts pounding. My hands get damp on the steering wheel if I’m driving, or on the armrest if someone else is driving. It’s like this rush of fear comes up all at once, before we’ve even reached the span.

So I wouldn’t say every single bridge causes the same intensity, but the ones that matter—the ones I think of as bridges in that frightening sense—yes, the reaction is pretty automatic once crossing them seems unavoidable.
